title: TikTok Script for Personal Trainers: 36 Ready-to-Film Ideas
markdown:
# TikTok Script for Personal Trainers: 36 Ready-to-Film Ideas

At 6:42 a.m., the workout is filmed, the clips are trimmed, and the empty script field is still blinking. You know how to coach the movement; you just need words that make a stranger stop, understand the point, and know what to do next.

This page gives you 36 TikTok script starters for personal trainers, plus a simple way to choose and test one. Use the bracketed fields before filming so the claim stays true to your coaching and your clients.

## Form fixes

### 1. Squat depth

**Hook:** “Your squat may not need to go lower. It may need this.”

**Beats:** Show the current squat → name the limitation you observe → demonstrate one setup change → invite viewers to try it with a bodyweight squat.

### 2. Push-up setup

**Hook:** “If push-ups hurt your wrists, check this before you quit them.”

**Beats:** Show hand position → show a supported variation → explain who should use it → CTA: “Save this for your next upper-body day.”

### 3. Deadlift start

**Hook:** “The bar is not the first thing to fix in your deadlift.”

**Beats:** Start with foot position → show the tension cue → demonstrate one rep → ask viewers which part feels hardest.

### 4. Lunge balance

**Hook:** “Wobbling in lunges? Make this change before adding weight.”

**Beats:** Show the unstable version → widen or shorten the stance as appropriate → show the controlled version → give one self-check.

### 5. Plank form

**Hook:** “A longer plank is not always a better plank.”

**Beats:** Show the common compensation → show a shorter, cleaner hold → explain the cue → CTA: “Try [ADD: your hold duration] with this position.”

### 6. Row technique

**Hook:** “If you only feel rows in your arms, start here.”

**Beats:** Show the arm-only pull → set the torso position → demonstrate the pull path → name the feeling to look for.

## Beginner confidence

### 7. First gym session

**Hook:** “Your first gym workout does not need 10 exercises.”

**Beats:** Name three movements → explain the order → show one set of each → ask viewers to save the plan.

### 8. Starting with bodyweight

**Hook:** “You do not need equipment to begin training this week.”

**Beats:** Show a squat, incline push-up, and hip hinge → give a beginner-friendly starting point → state how to progress → CTA: “Pick one day to begin.”

### 9. Feeling watched

**Hook:** “Nobody taught you the hardest part of the gym: walking in.”

**Beats:** Describe the first five minutes → show a simple warm-up station → give a three-exercise plan → remind viewers that a plan reduces guesswork.

### 10. Getting back after a break

**Hook:** “Coming back after a break? Do less than your motivation wants.”

**Beats:** Name the temptation to restart at full volume → give a smaller first-session template → show a recovery check → CTA: “Use [ADD: your progression rule] next week.”

### 11. Choosing weights

**Hook:** “Here is one way to choose a starting weight without guessing.”

**Beats:** Demonstrate a test set → define the form standard → explain when to adjust → invite viewers to log what happened.

### 12. Rest days

**Hook:** “A rest day is part of training, not proof you failed.”

**Beats:** Name the training signal → show low-intensity options → explain the individual limit → ask viewers what recovery looks like for them.

## Busy-schedule training

### 13. Ten-minute session

**Hook:** “Have 10 minutes? Train this instead of waiting for an hour.”

**Beats:** Show the timer → demonstrate three movements → explain the work/rest format as [ADD: your format] → CTA: “Save it for the next busy day.”

### 14. Desk-to-workout transition

**Hook:** “If work drains your energy, remove this decision after 5 p.m.”

**Beats:** Show clothes or equipment prepared ahead → show the first movement → explain the smallest useful session → ask viewers what they can prepare tonight.

### 15. Hotel workout

**Hook:** “No gym on this trip? Use the floor, a chair, and [ADD: available item].”

**Beats:** Show the space → demonstrate three substitutions → include a safety note for the surface → CTA: “Adapt it to your room.”

### 16. Lunch-break training

**Hook:** “Your lunch break can fit movement without becoming a second job.”

**Beats:** Show the first minute → offer a short circuit → explain how to scale it → invite viewers to choose one movement.

### 17. Missed workout

**Hook:** “Missing one workout does not require a punishment workout.”

**Beats:** State the missed-session scenario → show the next planned session → explain why you resume rather than cram → CTA: “Return to the next useful step.”

### 18. Morning routine

**Hook:** “The workout is easier when the decision happened last night.”

**Beats:** Show prep the evening before → show the first morning cue → offer a tiny session → ask viewers what their trigger will be.

## Strength and progression

### 19. Progressive overload

**Hook:** “Progressive overload is more than putting more plates on the bar.”

**Beats:** Show one exercise → name possible progress markers → explain how you record one → CTA: “Choose one metric for [ADD: your exercise].”

### 20. Reps versus weight

**Hook:** “Should you add reps or weight first? Start with your target.”

**Beats:** State the training goal → compare two progression choices → show one example using [ADD: exercise] → name the limit: form still governs the decision.

### 21. Training log

**Hook:** “Your next workout should not depend on memory.”

**Beats:** Show a simple log → name the three fields to record → demonstrate a before/after entry → CTA: “Write down today’s final set.”

### 22. Plateau check

**Hook:** “Before you call it a plateau, check these three things.”

**Beats:** Show training consistency, recovery, and progression records → explain what each reveals → suggest one change at a time.

### 23. Tempo work

**Hook:** “Before adding load, slow this part of the rep down.”

**Beats:** Show the usual rep → show the controlled phase → explain what you are observing → invite viewers to test it with a safe load.

### 24. Exercise substitutions

**Hook:** “The best substitute is not the trendiest exercise. It solves the same job.”

**Beats:** Name the original movement’s purpose → show an alternative → explain who might choose it → CTA: “Tell me what equipment you have.”

## Mobility and movement prep

### 25. Warm-up purpose

**Hook:** “Your warm-up does not need to make you tired.”

**Beats:** Show one movement-specific drill → connect it to the day’s lift → demonstrate the first work set → name the honest limit: warm-ups are not a cure-all.

### 26. Tight hips

**Hook:** “If your hips feel tight after sitting, do not stretch on autopilot.”

**Beats:** Show the moment you notice it → demonstrate one controlled movement → explain what you are checking → CTA: “Use the version that feels stable for you.”

### 27. Shoulder prep

**Hook:** “Before overhead work, I look for this movement first.”

**Beats:** Show the screen or drill → explain what it informs in today’s training → show a regression → remind viewers to work within their comfortable range.

### 28. Posture myth

**Hook:** “One ‘perfect posture’ is not the goal. Options are.”

**Beats:** Show two comfortable positions → explain changing positions through the day → give one movement break → ask viewers when they feel most stiff.

### 29. Ankle mobility

**Hook:** “Your squat setup may be asking more from your ankles than you realize.”

**Beats:** Show the observed limitation → show one assessment cue → demonstrate a modification → CTA: “Use the option that keeps your feet stable.”

### 30. Cool-down

**Hook:** “A cool-down is useful when it answers a real need.”

**Beats:** Name the need—downshifting, a transition, or a movement you enjoy → show a brief routine → avoid promising a universal outcome.

## Coaching decisions and client trust

### 31. Why plans differ

**Hook:** “Two clients can have the same goal and need different first workouts.”

**Beats:** Compare two fictional starting situations without identifying anyone → name the factors that change the plan → show the shared principle → CTA: “Your starting point matters.”

### 32. Scale without shame

**Hook:** “A regression is not the easy version. It is the right version for today.”

**Beats:** Show two versions of the same movement → explain the decision rule → show how progression can happen → invite viewers to choose control.

### 33. Coaching cue

**Hook:** “A cue only works if the person can use it on the next rep.”

**Beats:** Show a vague cue → replace it with one actionable cue → demonstrate the next rep → ask viewers which wording clicks.

### 34. When to refer out

**Hook:** “A good coach knows when training advice is not enough.”

**Beats:** State the boundary in plain language → explain that concerns outside your scope need an appropriate qualified professional → show how you modify or pause the session when needed.

### 35. Client goal check-in

**Hook:** “Before changing a program, ask this question.”

**Beats:** Ask: “What has changed since we last checked in?” → name schedule, energy, and preference as possible answers → show how one answer changes a plan.

### 36. Training consistency

**Hook:** “The best plan is the one your real week can hold.”

**Beats:** Contrast an ideal schedule with a realistic one → show a minimum session → explain how to build from consistency → CTA: “Write your real available days below.”

## How to pick one script and test it

Choose the script by the problem your audience can recognize fastest. A beginner who fears the gym needs a different opening from someone trying to refine a deadlift. Start with one audience, one situation, and one action you want them to take.

Then make the claim specific enough to demonstrate. Film the problem, the coaching decision, and the next step. If you cannot show the proof or explain the limit in a short video, narrow the claim.

Test one variable at a time. Keep the topic and practical value steady, then try a different hook, opening shot, or call to action. Review the comments and saves alongside your own coaching standard: the useful script is the one that attracts the right question and gives an honest answer.

## FAQ

### How long should a TikTok script for a personal trainer be?

Make it only as long as the demonstration needs. A simple form cue may need a hook, one visual comparison, and one next step; a training-plan explanation may need more beats. Write the beats before writing every word.

### Can I use these ideas if I coach online?

Yes. Replace in-person references with the equipment, space, and decision points your online clients actually have. Do not imply an individual assessment when you have not performed one.

### What should I say at the end of the video?

Ask for one relevant action: save the drill, comment with available equipment, or try a defined variation. Match the CTA to the lesson instead of adding a generic sales line.

### How do I avoid making claims I cannot support?

Describe what you observe, what you demonstrate, and the limit of the advice. Use your own verified numbers only, and write a blank such as [ADD: your number] until you can substantiate it.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the format you can send and receive:

**You send:** "A 30-second TikTok about why cold email still works in 2026."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Angle:** the single sharpest claim the video makes about cold email in 2026.
- **Hooks (3, one marked RECOMMENDED):**
  1. *Contrarian* — "Everyone says cold email is dead. It isn't." (RECOMMENDED, with the reason it works)
  2. *Question* — "Why did this cold email get a 40% reply rate?"
  3. *Stat-style* — a hook built only from facts you supplied.
- **Timed script table:** voiceover · on-screen text · visual/shot cue, beat by beat, HOOK → BUILD → PAYOFF → CTA.
- **Caption:** 4–6 hashtags plus one filming or posting tip.
